points: A two-judge Supreme Court Bench in Dr. Jaya Thakur vs Union of India delivered a split verdict on the 2023 Act governing the appointment of the CEC and ECs.
The core issue is that the 2023 Act gives appointment power to a panel dominated by the Prime Minister and a Union Minister, overriding the Baranwal ruling.
Justice Dipankar Datta held the Act must be tested against the Baranwal judgment, while Justice Satish Chandra Sharma referred the matter to a Constitution Bench.
The judges jointly sought an early hearing by a Constitution Bench on September 23, 2026, though petitioners criticized the delay.
A controversy arose over an undisclosed link where Justice Sharma’s son served as empanelled standing counsel for the ECI in the Madhya Pradesh High Court.
Petitioners filed recall petitions to nullify Justice Sharma's order, citing judicial ethics codes and the Rupa Ashok Hurra vs Ashok Hurra precedent.

The author concludes that Parliament should repeal the 2023 Act, judges must make written disclosures of family links, and a neutral body should select election umpires.
sum.text:
The choice of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and Election Commissioners (ECs) was to be shielded from the executive after Anoop Baranwal vs Union of India (2023) , yet a 2023 law handing it back to a government led panel remains in force. In Dr. Jaya Thakur vs Union of India , a two judge Bench of the Supreme Court delivered a split verdict on that law, leaving it to a Constitution Bench.
What it is: The CEC and ECs run elections as neutral umpires . A Constitution Bench in Baranwal held that a committee with executive predominance , one the government of the day controls, cannot select them, much like one team cannot pick the referee.
The 2023 Act: The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 gives selection to the Prime Minister , a Union Minister he chooses and the Leader of the Opposition .
Government majority: The Prime Minister and his Minister form two thirds of the committee, so the Opposition leader can always be outvoted.
Lifelong immunity: The Act also gives the CEC and ECs lifelong immunity for their acts and words in office.
The takeaway: Whoever controls the selection committee decides who runs elections.
Justice Dipankar Datta: Baranwal settled the position, so the Act must be tested against it. A panel led by the Prime Minister and his Minister has the executive predominance Baranwal barred.
Justice Satish Chandra Sharma: The issues were important enough to need a reference to a larger Constitution Bench .
Common order: On September 23, 2026 , the judges jointly sought an early hearing by a Constitution Bench.
Delay as failure: Counsel for the petitioners calls the reference an “institutional confession” that the Court failed to decide in time.
Undisclosed link: Justice Sharma’s son has served as empanelled standing counsel , a lawyer on the regular panel, for the Election Commission of India (ECI) in the Madhya Pradesh High Court. The link went undisclosed, a possible conflict of interest .
Recall petitions: Petitions in the Supreme Court now seek to recall and nullify Justice Sharma’s order.
Rupa Ashok Hurra vs Ashok Hurra (2002): A Constitution Bench indicated that a judge’s failure to disclose a link with the subject or the parties vitiates , or taints, the judgment, so it warrants a revisit.

India has moved from food scarcity to production, but food security also depends on nutrition, climate resilience, distribution and access to food.
Global Hunger Amid Food Abundance: Despite sufficient agricultural output, millions cannot afford nutritious diets. In 2025, a healthy diet cost an average of $4.28 per person per day, compared with the international extreme poverty line of $3 under purchasing power parity (PPP).
Climate Risks, Conflict and Economic Shocks: Climate change reduces crop yields and disrupts growing seasons, while wars damage harvests, displace farmers and interrupt supply chains. Economic shocks and food-price inflation further weaken purchasing power.

sum.text:
India has launched its bid for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) for 2028-29 , with the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) voting in June 2027 . sum.text:
The Centre’s decision to let its flagship urban livelihoods scheme lapse without a successor is injudicious and perplexing. This is particularly so given the positive impact that the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana- National Urban Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NULM) has had on the social and financial empowerment of women. Since its launch in 2014, the scheme has helped create 10.02 lakh self-help groups (SHGs), covering more than one crore women across cities. To risk leaving these beneficiaries adrift for want of continued support would be to betray the promise contained in slogans about women-led development invoked by parties across the spectrum.
Significantly, concerns over funding and the policy vacuum created by the end of NULM in October 2024, cut across party lines. Of the five states that have flagged the issue — Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Tripura — only the first two are Opposition-ruled. All five have sought funding to ensure continued support to SHGs and prevent disruption to their access to institutional credit and bank linkages. Addressing these concerns is critical to the larger goals of poverty alleviation and support to women’s entrepreneurship. There is ample evidence of SHGs’ capacity to advance women’s social and economic empowerment — by improving access to credit and skills, building financial literacy and leadership, and increasing self-confidence and mobility. The impact of initiatives such as Didi ki Rasoi and Bank Sakhis under Bihar’s JEEViKA scheme shows how such programmes can put money in women’s hands while shifting them from dependent household roles to decision-makers. Kerala’s Kudumbashree offers an even more expansive model, evolving from credit groups into a network involved in community kitchens, waste collection and training SHGs in other states.
States, too, must do their part. They have found resources for cash-transfer schemes; they must prioritise programmes for women that build enduring economic capacity. SHGs are institutions through which women acquire skills, networks, and a greater say in households and communities. To ensure these gains are sustained, efforts must be directed towards ensuring access to training, mentorship and institutional support. Going forward, it is not enough to expand SHG numbers — investment must also be made in the human resources, infrastructure, credit linkages and market networks that allow them to thrive.

Less than a month after the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was signed into law by US President Donald Trump, he has struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel supplies into global markets . The late senator Lindsey Graham’s bill was meant to impose new sanctions and tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas, choking off the revenue that funds the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine. Trump’s deal does the opposite. It will directly bankroll that war and undermine the international sanctions against Russia already in place. Ostensibly, the President wants to bring diesel prices down “for Americans and, indeed, the World”, as he put it in a social media post. But the real motive may not be hard to decipher. Poll after poll shows the Republican Party trailing the Democrats, and with midterm elections less than three weeks away, the likely goal is to placate American voters. The plan may not work. Energy analysts largely agree that the 36 million barrels of Russian diesel covered by the deal won’t bring down prices significantly, and many Republicans are pushing back. Trump has also made Ukraine’s position more difficult by demanding that Kyiv suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries, a move that would weaken its leverage.
From Trump administration officials such as Scott Bessent and Peter Navarro to the US President himself, India has been at the receiving end of Washington’s moral posturing over Russian energy imports. India was not only targeted by the Lindsey Graham Act, but also hit with an additional tariff penalty in August 2025 that prompted Indian refiners to reduce their purchases of Russian crude. Of course, energy security matters to the US. But it matters just as much to India. New Delhi should ask that its energy needs and costs be judged by the same standards as Washington’s. Throughout the war, India has maintained that its energy purchases are guided by national interest and the needs of its people. sum.text:
India has spent more than three decades building the constitutional architecture of local government. The 73 rd and 74 th Constitutional Amendments gave Panchayats and municipalities constitutional recognition and envisaged them as institutions of self-government. Yet India’s decentralisation remains unfinished. The problem is not simply that local governments do not receive enough money. It is that the institutional chain through which resources, responsibilities, and accountability are devolved remains weak. The Sixteenth Finance Commission’s treatment of State Finance Commissions (SFCs) brings this problem into sharp focus. The chain of fiscal federalism – and its fragile middle The Commission acknowledges the crucial constitutional role of SFCs in determining the resources available to rural and urban local bodies. At the same time, it points out that successive Finance Commissions have found it difficult to use SFC recommendations because many states do not constitute these commissions on time and the reports that are available vary considerably in their methodology, coverage, and quality. This leads to an uncomfortable but important question: if SFCs are too weak to inform fiscal devolution, should India bypass them – or make them work? The answer should be the latter. India’s fiscal federalism is usually discussed as a relationship between the Union and the states. Decentralisation, however, introduces a third tier of government, making the institutional architecture considerably more complex. The Union Finance Commission has a constitutional role in recommending measures for local bodies, while SFCs are expected to examine the finances of Panchayats and municipalities within individual states. In principle, this creates a powerful chain of fiscal federalism – from the Union to the state, from the State to local governments, and ultimately from local governments to citizens. The Supreme Court on Thursday held that a person who converts to Islam cannot claim reservation under the Muslim backward class (BC) category based on their former caste status.“Such conversion severs the legal foundation of an entitlement which is specifically conditioned upon membership of that Hindu social order," said the ruling of a two-judge Bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar. The top court held that a person who converts from a Hindu social order to a non-Hindu social order cannot claim affirmative action under Article 16(4) merely on the basis of social backwardness associated with his pre-conversion status. The apex court passed the ruling after the Tamil Nadu state government moved before it -- by filing an appeal -- against the HC order quashing its decision recognising seven backward class Muslim sects, allowing persons to be treated as backward class Muslims after converting.
The apex court said former caste or community status cannot automatically be transposed into the Muslim backward classes category, and a private religious body cannot conclusively determine statutory entitlement. Mumbai, Oct 15 (PTI) India's current account deficit narrowed to USD 5.2 billion in August from USD 6.1 billion a year ago, aided by a lower merchandise trade deficit and higher surpluses in services trade, according to preliminary data released by the RBI on Thursday.
The net deficit in the merchandise trade account declined to USD 26.6 billion in August from USD 27.6 billion in the same month last year.
Merchandise exports rose to USD 44.7 billion in August from USD 35.1 billion a year ago, while imports increased to USD 71.3 billion from USD 62.7 billion, the RBI data showed.
The surplus in services trade increased to USD 16.5 billion in August from USD 15.6 billion a year ago. Services exports rose to USD 35.5 billion from USD 31.2 billion, while imports increased to USD 18.9 billion from USD 15.6 billion.
Net transfers, including remittances, increased to USD 12.8 billion in August from USD 12.2 billion a year ago, while the net deficit in the income account widened to USD 8 billion from USD 6.3 billion.
During April-August 2026, the current account deficit widened to USD 18.3 billion from USD 12.8 billion in the corresponding period of the previous year, according to the preliminary data on 'Developments in India's Balance of Payments for the Month of August 2026'.
The merchandise trade deficit increased to USD 146 billion during the five months from USD 124.7 billion a year ago, while the surplus in services trade rose to USD 85.8 billion from USD 79.9 billion in the year-ago period.
Net transfers also increased to USD 66.8 billion from USD 55.6 billion.
On the capital account, net foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows stood at USD 3.3 billion in August, compared with a net outflow of USD 0.1 billion a year ago.
Also, net foreign portfolio investment recorded an inflow of USD 1.7 billion, against an outflow of USD 2.6 billion in August 2025.
Net banking capital recorded an inflow of USD 64.7 billion in August, compared with an outflow of USD 4.7 billion a year ago.
Net non-resident Indian (NRI) deposits stood at USD 83 billion, against USD 1 billion in the same month last year.
The overall balance of payments recorded a surplus of USD 45.4 billion in August, compared with a deficit of USD 5.6 billion a year ago.
During April-August 2026, the overall balance of payments recorded a surplus of USD 58 billion, compared with a deficit of USD 0.8 billion in the corresponding period last year. PTI NKD HVA

The Karnataka High Court on Monday, October 12, struck down a 2022 law that increased reservations for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs), ruling that the enhanced quotas breached the constitutionally established 50% ceiling on reservations. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice KS Hemalekha declared Sections 3 and 4 of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and of Appointments or Posts in the Services under the State) Act, 2022, unconstitutional. The court held that taking the overall reservation beyond 50% violated the equality provisions of the Constitution.
The law, enacted by the previous BJP government led by Basavaraj Bommai, increased the SC quota from 15% to 17% and the ST quota from 3% to 7%. With the 32% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) remaining unchanged, the overall reservation in Karnataka rose from 50% to 56%.“Section 3 of the Act, insofar as it takes the aggregate reservation beyond the ceiling of 50%, is struck down as it violates Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution. Section 4 of the Act is also struck down as unconstitutional, as it violates Articles 14 and 16,” the Bench said in its order.
The judgment followed petitions challenging the constitutional validity of the law, including a public interest litigation filed by Raichur-based social worker Mahendra Kumar Mitra and a petition by civil engineering graduates H R Sagar and others. The latter challenged enhanced reservation in recruitment to posts in the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP). One of the central questions before the court was whether the state could exceed the 50% ceiling by citing the population and inadequate representation of backward communities.
The state had argued that more than 90% of Karnataka’s population belonged to SC, ST and OBC communities and that reservations should reflect their share of the population. Rejecting this argument, the Bench said the numerical strength of backward classes did not permit the state to breach the ceiling. “The subjective opinion of the state government that a backward class is not adequately represented in proportion to its population does not enable the state to exceed the limit of 50% (ceiling reservation), but only to provide for reservation within the said limit,” it said.

MUMBAI, Oct 15 (Reuters) - India's banking system deposits hit a record high of around 284 trillion rupees ($2.99 trillion) in the second half of September, central bank data showed on Thursday.
Deposits rose by 21.67 trillion rupees in the first six months of the financial year, with most of the increase seen between June and August, when the central bank's discounted swap window to attract dollar inflows was in place.
• Banking system deposits jumped by an aggregate of 20 trillion rupees from June 16 to August 31, according to data from the Reserve Bank of India.
• In June, the RBI announced a discounted swap window to attract foreign-currency deposits and encouraged lenders to raise cheaper deposits.
• The scheme saw inflows of around $133 billion and the deposit window was closed on August 31, a month earlier than planned.
• Deposits were also boosted by lenders' efforts to build funding buffers before the end of the quarter; the fortnight ended September 30 saw inflows of 7.73 trillion rupees.
• Overall deposits in the banking system as of September-end were up 8.4% as compared with March-end.
• Competition for deposits stayed contained, while the system was in surplus, CareEdge Ratings said in a note.
• "The October rate hike rules out further cuts in term deposit rates for now and is likely to push them up, as banks need to fund credit that is growing faster than deposits while the liquidity surplus shrinks," CareEdge added.

The Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras) has launched an ambitious mission to create three-dimensional (3D) atlases of more than 100 human brains at cellular resolution across the human lifespan. The initiative also includes the release of C-STROKE, the world's first human ischemic stroke atlas. Marking a significant milestone in India's neuroscience research, Prime Minister Narendra Modi dedicated the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre (SGBC) at IIT Madras to the nation during his visit to the institute on October 11.
The Prime Minister said the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre marks an important step towards advancing cutting-edge research and innovation in healthcare.
He also witnessed the launch of the Centre's mission to create 3D brain atlases at cellular resolution and the release of C-STROKE, a resource designed to advance research into ischemic stroke.
According to IIT Madras, the Centre combines advanced brain imaging, computing, and multidisciplinary scientific and technological expertise to make high-resolution brain maps accessible to researchers and medical professionals worldwide. These resources are expected to deepen understanding of brain structure and neurological diseases while opening new avenues for neuroscience and neuromedicine.
During the Prime Minister's visit, the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre released C-STROKE as an open-access global resource for studying ischemic stroke.
According to IIT Madras, the atlas bridges clinical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans with microscopic, whole-brain imaging, offering insights into stroke-related changes at the cellular level. It features more than 1,000 annotated brain sections and maps key cellular markers associated with neuronal health, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, hypoxia, and axonal injury.
Developed with support from IIT Madras alumnus V Prem Watsa, the atlas provides an open-access platform for researchers and clinicians worldwide to investigate cerebrovascular diseases and explore potential therapeutic targets.

The statements had also called for detained leaders of the Joint Awami Action Committee to have access to legal representation and their families, and had called for due process and fair trial. sum.text:
Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The National Green Tribunal (NGT), Central Zone Bench, Bhopal, directed all the concerned departments of Bhopal to submit detailed replies within two weeks on measures taken to control air pollution in Madhya Pradesh. It stressed strict compliance with Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) guidelines, state regulations and Supreme Court orders, particularly during festivals. The directions were issued on Tuesday in Original Application of Rashid Noor Khan vs State of Madhya Pradesh and Others, and uploaded on Wednesday.
Advocate of the applicant, Harshvardhan Tiwari, confirmed that the bench called for enforcement of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), with corrective measures implemented according to air quality levels. Authorities were also directed to ensure strict compliance with applicable regulations governing firecrackers to curb air and noise pollution during festivals. The next hearing is scheduled for November 18.
Bhopal PM10 levels decline 3%Data presented before the tribunal showed that Bhopal's annual average PM10 concentration declined from 113 micrograms per cubic metre in 2023-24 to 110 in 2024-25, a reduction of around 3%. In contrast, Indore's levels increased from 99 to 108 micrograms per cubic metre during the same period. Road dust identified as major pollutantA source apportionment study identified road dust, vehicular emissions, construction activities and open waste burning as major pollution sources.
The tribunal stressed targeted action at pollution hotspots, suction-based road cleaning, proper management of roadsides and footpaths, vehicle emission control, construction waste management and prevention of open waste burning. It also emphasised expanding continuous ambient air quality monitoring stations (CAAQMS) at suitable locations. Compliance report before next hearing.
The tribunal directed the respondents to submit detailed replies within two weeks and report compliance with its May 20, 2026, order. It also sought details of action taken on decisions of state-level and district-level committees. The bench emphasised that planning alone was insufficient and called for effective ground-level implementation, regular monitoring and time-bound compliance.
